Really this applies to all 'alt' sites as well.

Let's consider the common pattern, chronologically:

  • there is a website, let's call it A

  • A is becoming more restrictive, less enjoyable to use, not what it once was

  • site B is created, hailed as a better place for users than A

  • people notice that B seems to hold only 'fringe views' and is angry all the time

So what happened? Let's think about the content of both sides as a venn diagram. There's content that 'works' in A, content that will succeed by the site's given metric (votes, views, likes, number of people who see it). There's also content that works in B. The important idea here is that most content fits in the middle of the venn diagram, content that works in A as well as B. When B is created, the content that works only on B moves. This takes some effort, getting used to a new style, new interface. If there's no gain from moving sites, there's no sense in putting in the effort. The content that works on both sites has momentum, and wants to stay wherever it is.

Consider Voat and reddit.

Right-wing content is less and less tolerated on reddit, so there's a gain to be had by moving to voat.

Left-wing content is less tolerated on Voat, so it stays on reddit.

Apolitical content could work on either, so there's no motive for it to move either way. It stays put where it is, on reddit.

Hence why voat is mostly right-wing political content: there's no reason for already established apolitical content to come here, and an effort needed to move.
